title: Sucuklu yumurta
subtitle: Turkish spiced sausage with fried eggs
excerpt: Sucuklu yumurta is a Turkish breakfast of spiced beef sausage slices fried in a pan until their fat renders and they caramelise, then eggs cracked in alongside to cook in the same fat. Merguez is the closest widely-available equivalent to the Turkish sucuk.
sourceNotes: Aylin Oney Tan, A Taste of Sun and Fire: Gaziantep Cookery (2014). Sucuklu yumurta documented as a standard Turkish breakfast. Claudia Roden, Arabesque (2005). Turkish breakfast culture described, including the sucuk and egg combination.

content.text: Sucuklu yumurta is a Turkish breakfast of sliced spiced sausage fried until crisp and caramelised, then eggs cooked in the same rendered fat. The authentic sucuk is a dry-cured Turkish beef and lamb sausage heavily spiced with garlic, cumin, and fenugreek; merguez, the North African beef and lamb sausage, is the closest substitute and gives a similar result. No added oil is needed: the sausage releases enough fat to cook the eggs.

items.prepNote: sliced into 1 cm rounds (as a substitute for Turkish sucuk)

content.text: Serve with bread for scooping. If you can find Turkish sucuk in a Middle Eastern or Eastern European shop, use it: the flavour is more garlicky and funky than merguez.

Place the sliced {{merguez}} in a cold, dry frying pan. Set over a medium heat. As the pan warms, the fat will begin to render from the sausage. Cook for three to four minutes per side until the slices are deeply browned and slightly crispy at the edges, and the pan is slicked with rendered fat.
Push the sausage slices to the edges of the pan to make room. Crack {{eggs}} directly into the fat in the centre of the pan.
Cook the eggs sunny side up for two to three minutes until the whites are fully set and the yolks are still runny, or to your preference. Season with {{black-pepper}} and {{chilli-flakes}} if using.
Serve directly from the pan with bread. Scatter {{parsley-flat}} over if using.

items.symptom: The sausage is not releasing much fat
items.fix: Add a teaspoon of olive oil to the pan before the sausage to ensure the eggs have fat to cook in.

items.symptom: The egg whites are raw at the edges but the yolks are already overcooked
items.fix: After adding the eggs, reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pan with a lid for the last minute to help the whites set without overcooking the yolks.

items.symptom: The sausage is releasing a lot of liquid rather than browning
items.cause: Pan too crowded or heat too low
items.fix: Cook in a single layer. The slices need space to brown. Increase the heat and move them less frequently.

items.cause: The rendered fat of spiced sausage is very rich
items.fix: Tip off some of the rendered fat before adding the eggs, leaving just enough to coat the pan.

content.text: Sucuklu yumurta is a staple of the extended Turkish breakfast known as kahvalti, which typically includes cheeses, olives, honey, clotted cream, fresh tomatoes, cucumbers, bread, and several small hot dishes including eggs and sausage. The sucuk itself is a spiced, dry-cured sausage made from beef, lamb, or a mixture, heavily seasoned with garlic, cumin, allspice, and fenugreek. It is sold in rings or links and keeps for weeks in the fridge because of the curing process. In Turkey it is also commonly used in gozleme (flatbread) fillings, pide toppings, and omelettes.
